title: Unit Testing Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Unit Testing lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: One small behaviour
entries.summary: A unit is a small piece of behaviour, often a function. Test what it returns for a clear input.
notes: Do not test several unrelated functions in one unclear check.

entries.name: Arrange act assert
entries.summary: Arrange prepares input. Act runs the code. Assert checks the result. These three steps make a test easy to read.

example.code:
const input = 3; // arrange
const actual = input * input; // act
console.log(actual === 9); // assert

notes: Do not calculate the expected result using the same buggy function you are testing.

entries.name: Name the rule
entries.summary: A useful test name says the rule and the situation. Someone should understand a failure without opening every line of code.
notes: Names such as test1 hide the reason for the test.

entries.name: Compare values carefully
entries.summary: Equality checks need to match the data you care about. Two different objects are not the same object even if their fields match.
notes: Use a test runner's deep-value matcher when checking object contents.

entries.name: Boundary cases in a unit
entries.summary: Choose a value where a rule changes. Test both sides so a wrong comparison sign is visible.

example.code:
const passes = score => score >= 5;
console.log(passes(4) === false, passes(5) === true);

notes: Testing only a very high score misses a wrong boundary.

entries.name: Test expected errors
entries.summary: Some functions should reject bad input. Check that the rejection happens and that its message is useful.
notes: A test that catches every error but checks nothing can pass for the wrong reason.

entries.name: Fresh data for each test
entries.summary: Tests should not depend on the order they run. Make fresh input when a function changes its input.
notes: A shared mutable list can make tests pass alone but fail together.

entries.name: Inject a dependency
entries.summary: A dependency is another function or object that code uses. Passing it in lets a test choose a simple, predictable replacement.

example.code:
function greetFrom(getName) { return "Hi " + getName(); }
console.log(greetFrom(() => "Asha") === "Hi Asha");

notes: Do not call a real paid service just to test a greeting.

entries.name: Spies record calls
entries.summary: A spy records how a dependency was used. This helps test actions such as saving a message.
notes: Checking only call count misses a wrong argument.

entries.name: Wait for async work
entries.summary: Async work finishes later. A test must wait for its promise before checking the result.

example.code:
async function getScore() { return 8; }
getScore().then(score => console.log(score === 8));

notes: A test can finish too early if you forget to wait.

entries.name: Use several cases
entries.summary: A table of cases checks the same rule with several inputs. Keep each expected result easy to see.

example.code:
const cases = [[0, 0], [2, 4], [-3, -6]];
for (const [input, expected] of cases) console.log(input * 2 === expected);

notes: More repeated cases do not help if they all test the same uninteresting path.

entries.name: Read a failure before fixing it
entries.summary: A failure is evidence that actual and expected results differ. Check the requirement before changing either the code or the expected answer.
notes: Do not change an expectation only to turn the test green.
